editorial.bruteForceApproach: Enumerate all 2^n subsets, compute each sum, and count those equal to target.
editorial.optimalApproach: Set ways[0] = 1. For each candidate, add ways[sum-value] into ways[sum] while iterating sums downward.

problems.title: Rising Corridor
problems.story: A gallery hangs its collection along a single corridor in the order the pieces were acquired. That ordering is a curatorial rule and cannot be changed: the corridor is meant to be read as a history, so a piece acquired later never hangs before one acquired earlier. The incoming director wants the corridor to read as a rising line, each piece on display taller than the one before it. Pieces that spoil the line can go to storage, but the ones that stay keep their relative order, because that is the rule that cannot bend.
problems.statement:
You are given the height of each piece, in acquisition order.

You may send any pieces to storage. The pieces left on display keep their original relative order. The display is a rising line if each piece on it is strictly taller than the piece before it, so two pieces of equal height can never both stay: neither is taller than the other.

Return the largest number of pieces that can stay on display.

problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the largest number of pieces that can form a rising line without reordering them. Return 0 for an empty collection.

hints: Nothing is ever reordered, so the only decision is which pieces to keep. Storage is where the discarded ones go, not a place you can rearrange.
Fix the piece that ends the display. The best line ending there is one more than the best line ending at some earlier, strictly shorter piece.
That recurrence compares every piece with every earlier piece, which is quadratic and will not finish at two hundred thousand pieces. Ask what you actually need to remember from the earlier work.
For each possible line length, remember only the smallest height that can end a line of that length. Adding a piece either extends the longest line or improves one of those endings.
The list of smallest endings is always sorted, which is what lets you find the entry a new height belongs at with a binary search rather than a scan.

editorial.overview: Order is fixed and only removal is allowed, so the display is a subsequence of the acquisition order, and the rising rule makes it a strictly increasing one. The task is therefore the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, and the whole difficulty is getting that length without comparing every pair of pieces.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Let best[i] be the longest rising line that ends with piece i. Then best[i] is one plus the largest best[j] over every earlier piece j that is strictly shorter, or one if there is no such piece. The answer is the largest best[i]. This is correct and costs O(n squared), which is about four times ten to the tenth comparisons at the top of the range and will not finish.
editorial.optimalApproach: Keep a list called tails, where tails[k] is the smallest height that can end a rising line of length k plus one. This list is always strictly increasing: a line of length k plus one contains a line of length k ending at a strictly smaller height, so tails[k] is strictly below tails[k plus one]. For each incoming height, binary search for the first entry that is greater than or equal to it. If there is none, the height extends the longest line and is appended. Otherwise it replaces that entry, because a line of that length can now end at a smaller height, which can only help later pieces. The answer is the final length of tails. Each piece costs one binary search, so the whole pass is O(n log n) time and O(n) space. Note that tails is not itself a valid display; only its length is meaningful.
editorial.correctnessProof: Two claims. First, tails stays sorted and each entry is achievable: appending happens only when the new height exceeds every entry, which extends a real line by one, and replacing sets tails[k] to a height that ends a line of length k plus one because everything before position k is unchanged and still strictly smaller. Second, tails[k] is minimal. Suppose some rising line of length k plus one ended at a height below tails[k]. Consider the moment its last piece was processed. The binary search would have found the first entry greater than or equal to that height at index k or lower and written it there, so tails[k] would already be at most that height. Since every entry is achievable and no achievable ending is smaller, the length of tails is exactly the length of the longest rising line. Strictness is carried entirely by searching for the first entry greater than or equal to the height rather than strictly greater, which is what stops equal heights extending a line.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n log n), where n is the number of pieces. One binary search over a list of at most n entries per piece.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the list of smallest endings.

The longest-increasing-subsequence pattern and its patience-sorting refinement are standard and named openly in the editorial; the story, wording, example values and test cases are original to this record. Coin change and maximum subarray sum were both considered and rejected under the distinctness rule: the first belongs to the hit-a-target-from-a-set family the library already covers twice, the second to the maximise-a-sum-over-a-selection family of the group this record replaces.

problems.title: Street Donation Planner
problems.story: Street Donation Planner is an independent Quadrantcode practice scenario. A planning team has reduced its observations to an integer sequence and needs a precise maximum nonadjacent total result before the next decision can be made.
problems.statement: Implement the required function for Street Donation Planner. Interpret the supplied sequence exactly as described in the input contract, compute the maximum nonadjacent total, and return only the requested integer. The function must handle boundary cases and the largest stated input without modifying any external state.
problems.inputFormat: values contains nonnegative rewards in their fixed left-to-right order.
problems.outputFormat: Return the maximum total reward obtainable without selecting adjacent positions.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The complete integer encoding described by this problem.

constraints: The result fits in signed 64-bit range.

hints: At each position, compare skipping it with taking it after the best result two positions back.
Only the previous two dynamic-programming states are needed.

editorial.overview: Use the recurrence best[i] = max(best[i-1], best[i-2] + values[i]) with two rolling variables.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Recursively choose or skip every position, rejecting branches that choose adjacent positions.
editorial.optimalApproach: Maintain the best total through the previous position and through the position before it, updating once per reward.
editorial.correctnessProof: Every valid optimal selection either omits the current position, giving the previous best, or includes it, forcing omission of the previous position and giving the two-back best plus current reward. Taking the maximum covers both exhaustive cases.

c11.referenceSolution: long long solve(const long long*v,int n){long long a=0,b=0;for(int i=0;i<n;i++){long long z=b>a+v[i]?b:a+v[i];a=b;b=z;}return b;}

cpp17.referenceSolution: long long solve(const vector<long long>&v){long long a=0,b=0;for(auto x:v){auto n=max(b,a+x);a=b;b=n;}return b;}

java.referenceSolution: static long solve(long[]v){long a=0,b=0;for(long x:v){long n=Math.max(b,a+x);a=b;b=n;}return b;}

javascript.referenceSolution: function solve(v){let a=0,b=0;for(const x of v){const n=Math.max(b,a+x);a=b;b=n;}return b;}
